facts.title: SP 800-61r3 reorganises incident response around CSF 2.0 functions
facts.fact: NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 (April 2025) replaces the four sequential phases used in Revision 2 (2012) - Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity - with guidance organised around the six CSF 2.0 functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. Revision 3 treats incident response as a continuous capability managed across the whole risk-management lifecycle, so containment, communication and lessons learned can overlap instead of waiting for a phase gate. Organisations still using the 2012 model can map each phase to the newer functions, but plans and programme reporting should state which model and revision they follow.
details: Revision 2 remains widely taught and is a useful mental model even though Revision 3 supersedes it.
The Respond function covers incident management, analysis, mitigation, reporting and communication.
Revision 3 is published as a CSF 2.0 Community Profile and references the CSF 2.0 implementation examples.
pitfalls: Treating the r3 functions as a strict sequence, which reintroduces the phase-gate delay the revision was meant to remove.
Citing 'NIST 800-61' without a revision, leaving readers unsure whether the four-phase or CSF-aligned model is meant.

mcqs.question: Which statement best describes how SP 800-61r3 relates to the earlier four-phase incident response lifecycle?
options: It keeps the four phases and adds a fifth governance phase.
It reorganises guidance around the six CSF 2.0 functions and treats incident response as continuous.
It removes the need for preparation because detection tooling now covers it.
It applies only to federal agencies in the United States.
mcqs.rationale: Revision 3 aligns incident response with CSF 2.0 (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) and frames it as an ongoing capability rather than a strict sequence, while the four-phase model from Revision 2 remains a usable mapping.

facts.title: What preparation must exist before an incident starts
facts.fact: Preparation is the phase where constraints are still negotiable: a named incident commander with deputies, an approved plan with scenario playbooks, offline copies of contact and escalation data, out-of-band communication that does not depend on possibly compromised mail or chat, an asset and identity inventory, known-good logging baselines, pre-staged forensic tooling, and pre-agreed legal, privacy, insurer and external-IR relationships. It also covers tested backups and documented decision rights, because during an incident nobody has time to negotiate who may isolate a production cluster. Preparation is never finished: it is re-validated after every exercise and every real incident.
details: Playbooks should exist per scenario type (ransomware, business email compromise, credential theft, insider, web compromise, cloud) rather than as one generic document.
Out-of-band contact data must remain usable when email, single sign-on and the VPN are all suspect.
Contact and escalation lists should be printable and stored offline, not only in the wiki.

mcqs.question: Which item is most valuable specifically because it does not depend on infrastructure that may already be compromised?
options: A SIEM dashboard with live alerting
An offline copy of contacts, procedures and out-of-band communication details
A vulnerability scanner with current signatures
A cloud-hosted incident ticketing system
mcqs.rationale: During identity or mail compromise the normal collaboration stack may be untrustworthy or unavailable, so offline contact data, procedures and an out-of-band channel keep the response running.

misconceptions.claim: Adopting a commercial incident response vendor's PDF playbook completes preparation.
misconceptions.correction: A playbook is only a draft until roles, decision rights, contact data, tooling access and backups have been tested against your own estate; untested documents routinely fail at the first inject, for example when nobody can reach the person authorised to isolate a system.

facts.title: Severity should follow business impact, not technical novelty
facts.fact: Severity classification determines who is woken, what money is spent and which regulators are told, so it must be anchored in business impact: sensitivity and volume of data, number of identities and hosts, involvement of privileged or service accounts, safety and availability effects, contractual and regulatory exposure, and whether the actor is still active. Technical signals such as a critical CVE or a high-signature antivirus alert are inputs, not the classification. Declaration criteria should be written with concrete examples, a named declaring authority and a deputy, and a documented path to upgrade or downgrade. Ambiguity produces over-declaration and, far more often, costly under-declaration while analysts wait for certainty.
details: A usable four-tier example: P1 confirmed active compromise of crown-jewel data or safety-relevant systems; P2 confirmed compromise with limited scope; P3 credible suspicion not yet confirmed; P4 policy violation or no impact after triage.
The declaring authority must be reachable out of band and able to act without convening a committee.
Record the rationale for the assigned severity, because it is reviewed after the incident.

mcqs.question: An analyst finds a critical-rated vulnerability on an internet-facing appliance but no evidence of exploitation. What is the most defensible severity driver?
options: The CVSS score alone, because it is the industry standard
The business impact if exploited, combined with current evidence of exploitation and exposure
The vendor's marketing severity label
Whether the appliance is mentioned in a news article
mcqs.rationale: CVSS describes technical severity in the abstract; incident severity depends on impact to this organisation plus evidence and exposure. A critical CVE on an unexposed, patched-in-days system is not the same incident as confirmed exploitation of a crown-jewel service.

misconceptions.claim: Declaring an incident too early damages credibility, so teams should wait until compromise is proven.
misconceptions.correction: Waiting for proof is the more common and more expensive error: containment, evidence preservation and notification clocks all start late. A documented suspicion-level tier lets the organisation respond proportionately and downgrade if triage clears it.

facts.title: Detection and analysis: validate, scope, then decide
facts.fact: Triage is a loop rather than a checklist: confirm the alert is real by checking rule logic and known-good activity, establish scope (which identities, hosts, accounts and time window), decide whether containment can wait while evidence is collected, and record the reasoning. The most expensive mistake is remediating the first visible host before answering how many others exist. Pivot on identity and logon activity, process lineage including parent and grandparent, file hashes, scheduled tasks and services, and network destinations. Scope drives severity, and severity drives who is told and how fast.
details: Write the working hypothesis down and then look for evidence that falsifies it; untested hypotheses become blind spots.
Check whether the same tooling or account appears in other telemetry sources before concluding the case is a single host.
Time-box triage and escalate on scope rather than on certainty.

mcqs.question: During triage of a suspected endpoint compromise, which action should come before remediating the first affected host?
options: Reimaging the host to remove the malware
Establishing scope across identities, hosts and the time window
Sending a company-wide notification
Closing the alert as a false positive
mcqs.rationale: Scope determines whether this is a single-host event or a campaign, and it drives severity, containment choice and notification. Reimaging first destroys evidence and frequently leaves other compromised hosts untouched.

facts.title: Evidence preservation and chain of custody
facts.fact: Evidence handling has to survive scrutiny months later, so the basics are non-negotiable: collect the most volatile data first, use a hardware or software write blocker before touching a disk, hash at acquisition and re-hash before analysis, keep the original sealed and work from verified copies, and record for every item who collected it, when in UTC, where, why, with what tool and version, and the resulting hash. Chain-of-custody records must show every transfer of physical or logical custody, including internal handoffs between analysts. Preservation decisions made in the first hour are the ones challenged in reviews, tribunals and courts.
details: A SHA-256 recorded at acquisition and re-verified later detects accidental alteration; it does not prove the evidence was untouched before acquisition.
Store images on media with integrity checking, and document storage location and who has access.
Do not boot a suspect disk, run antivirus over it, or open files directly from it on an analysis workstation.

mcqs.question: What does a matching SHA-256 taken at acquisition and re-checked before analysis actually demonstrate?
options: That the suspect never committed the act under investigation
That the image has not changed since the hash was recorded
That the acquisition tool is court-approved
That the original disk was never written to before acquisition
mcqs.rationale: A hash comparison proves integrity from the moment of hashing onward. It says nothing about events before acquisition, tool approval, or guilt, which is why write blocking and contemporaneous records matter separately.

misconceptions.claim: Once the image hash matches, the evidence is automatically admissible.
misconceptions.correction: Admissibility is a legal determination that also depends on lawful collection, documented custody, tool reliability and relevance. A matching hash supports integrity but cannot cure an undocumented break in custody or an unlawful search.

facts.title: Communications, legal and privacy escalation during an incident
facts.fact: Communications fail in predictable ways: too many voices, technical detail leaking to customers, and legal or privacy teams learning about a personal-data incident from the press. Appoint one external spokesperson and one internal coordinator, agree a cadence for holding statements, and route anything touching personal data, regulated data, contracts or criminal conduct through counsel and the privacy office immediately. In many jurisdictions counsel should direct the investigation so that work product can be argued as privileged, and privilege markings must be applied deliberately rather than pasted onto every document. Never speculate publicly about cause, actor or scope while the facts are still moving.
details: GDPR Article 33 requires notifying the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal-data breach unless it is unlikely to result in a risk to rights and freedoms.
Notification duties vary by sector and country; the privacy office decides, not the incident commander.
Prepare internal, customer, regulator and media templates before an incident so the first statement is not drafted under pressure.

mcqs.question: Why is a single external spokesperson combined with a single internal coordinator preferable to letting technical leads brief customers directly?
options: It reduces the chance of inconsistent, speculative or legally risky statements while keeping internal decisions coordinated
It is required by ISO 27001 certification
It guarantees the organisation will avoid regulatory notification
It prevents the attacker from learning about the response
mcqs.rationale: Technical leads often disclose unverified detail that becomes a public commitment or a legal problem. A single voice with an agreed cadence keeps statements consistent and reviewed, while an internal coordinator ensures decisions and facts flow to the right teams.

pitfalls: Sending the first external statement before counsel and privacy have reviewed the facts that are being asserted.
Allowing the incident bridge to be the only record, so nothing is attributable or reproducible later.

facts.title: Legal hold, spoliation risk and notification duties
facts.fact: Once litigation, a regulator inquiry or a criminal referral is reasonably anticipated, a legal hold must suspend routine deletion: mailbox retention policies, log rotation, backup expiry, ticketing cleanup and laptop wipes. Destroying evidence after a hold is issued risks spoliation sanctions and adverse inference, and in some jurisdictions criminal liability. Notification clocks differ sharply: GDPR's 72-hour supervisory-authority deadline, US state breach laws with varying definitions of personal information, and the US SEC rule requiring public companies to file an Item 1.05 Form 8-K within four business days of determining that an incident is material. The incident commander should know which clocks are running, who owns each one, and what evidence each obligation requires.
details: A hold notice should identify custodians, data sources, date ranges and the person responsible for enforcement.
Preserve in place where possible, but verify that retention tooling and automatic deletion will not expire items during the hold.
Engagement with law enforcement is a strategy decision: it can preserve evidence and enable disruption, but it may complicate disclosure timelines and control of the investigation.

mcqs.question: An organisation reasonably anticipates litigation and issues a legal hold. Which action is most likely to create spoliation risk?
options: Hashing and imaging the affected laptops before returning them to users
Allowing a 30-day mailbox retention policy to delete the custodian's messages during the hold
Exporting audit logs to a separate evidence store
Documenting which analysts accessed the evidence
mcqs.rationale: A legal hold suspends routine destruction. Letting an automated retention policy delete relevant messages during the hold destroys evidence the organisation is obliged to preserve, which is the essence of spoliation.

pitfalls: Assuming a cloud provider's default retention is sufficient; many SaaS audit logs expire in 30 to 180 days unless exported.
Letting the incident response vendor delete its working copies at case closure before legal confirms no hold applies.

facts.title: Ransomware playbook: scope, isolate, assume theft
facts.fact: The first moves in a ransomware incident are to confirm scope, isolate affected systems at the network layer without powering them off so memory and encryption artifacts survive, preserve at least one encrypted host with its ransom note untouched, and verify whether backups are intact and immutable before promising restoration. Modern extortion is usually double: data is stolen before encryption, so hunting for exfiltration through proxy, DNS and cloud logs is part of containment, not an afterthought. Payment decisions belong to executives with legal and sanctions advice, because paying does not guarantee decryption and may raise sanctions exposure. Recovery should start from a rebuilt, patched estate rather than restoring over a compromised identity plane.
details: If Active Directory compromise is suspected, reset the krbtgt account twice, separated by more than the domain's maximum ticket lifetime (10 hours by default), so existing tickets expire.
Immutable or offline backups are the control that changes the outcome; verify restore, not just backup success.
Expect accounts, scheduled tasks and remote-access paths created by the actor to survive reimaging of endpoints.

logs.context: EDR detection on a file server before encryption
logs.text:
2026-03-04T02:41:09Z host-fs02 4688 process: vssadmin.exe
  cmdline: vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet
  user: EXAMPLE\svc-backup
2026-03-04T02:43:55Z host-fs02 EDR: mass file rename detected (2143 files in 60s) by process encryptor.tmp.exe
logs.reading: Shadow-copy deletion followed within minutes by mass renames is the classic pre-encryption sequence (T1490 then T1486). The service account running vssadmin is itself a finding: either it is compromised or the binary is being run under stolen credentials. Isolate the file server's network path immediately and capture memory before any reboot.

mcqs.question: Why is powering off a ransomware-affected server usually worse than network isolation?
options: Powering off voids the vendor warranty
It destroys volatile memory evidence and may trigger additional damage on reboot, while isolation stops spread but preserves state
Ransomware only encrypts while the machine is running
Powering off prevents backups from completing
mcqs.rationale: Shutdown discards memory-resident evidence such as keys and injected code, and some ransomware or its persistence can cause further damage at next boot. Network isolation limits spread while keeping the host available for memory capture and forensic imaging.

misconceptions.claim: If backups restore successfully, there is no need to investigate exfiltration.
misconceptions.correction: Double-extortion actors steal data before encrypting. Restoring service without scoping theft leaves the organisation exposed to a second extortion demand, regulatory notification obligations and reputational harm, all of which require evidence from proxy, DNS, SaaS and endpoint logs.

facts.title: Business email compromise leaves identity and mail-flow artifacts
facts.fact: Business email compromise often involves no malware at all: an attacker with valid credentials or a stolen session token reads mail, creates hidden inbox rules, adds forwarding, registers an extra MFA method and sometimes grants OAuth consent to a malicious application. Investigation therefore focuses on identity and mail-flow telemetry: sign-in logs with unfamiliar locations, devices or user agents, mailbox audit events for rule creation and delegation, new application consents, and sent items containing changed bank details. Containment means revoking sessions and refresh tokens, removing rules and forwarding, resetting credentials, reviewing MFA registration, and warning finance and the counterparty bank before the next payment run.
details: A hidden rule that moves messages to an obscure folder both hides replies and preserves the attacker's access to thread history.
Check for SendAs and FullAccess delegation grants, not only inbox rules.
Payment-fraud recovery depends on speed: banks may be able to recall funds only within a short window after transfer.

2026-03-02T18:07:21Z New-InboxRule

  ClientIP: 198.51.100.77

The account is being used to intercept payment discussions. Revoke sessions, remove the rule and forwarding, then review sent items and any authentication changes.

mcqs.question: Which artifact most directly indicates that a mailbox is being used to intercept invoice conversations?
options: A new inbox rule that moves messages containing 'invoice' to an unused folder and marks them read
An increase in mailbox storage consumption
A user changing their display name
A mobile device enrolling in MDM
mcqs.rationale: Rules that conceal specific business conversations while marking them read are a hallmark of BEC, because they hide both the attacker's activity and the replies from the real recipient. Storage growth and display-name changes are weak, ambiguous signals.

facts.title: Credential theft response must evict sessions, not just reset passwords
facts.fact: Stolen credentials come in several forms - plaintext or cached passwords, Kerberos tickets, browser-stored secrets, LSASS memory dumps, and session cookies or OAuth refresh tokens - and each needs a different eviction step. A password reset does not invalidate a stolen refresh token or an existing Kerberos ticket, which is why incidents recur days after an apparently clean reset. Response should revoke sessions and tokens, remove attacker-registered MFA methods, rotate secrets and service-account credentials, and then hunt for the persistence the actor created while holding the account. For privileged identities, perform the reset from a clean, dedicated management workstation.
details: Service accounts and application secrets such as API keys and app registration credentials are frequently forgotten and are high value.
Check for newly created accounts, mailbox delegations and application consents after eviction.
Token theft through adversary-in-the-middle phishing survives both password and MFA changes until sessions are revoked.

logs.text:
2026-03-06T04:12:55Z Sign-in
  User: victim@example.internal
  App: Office 365 Exchange Online
  IP: 203.0.113.44
  Auth: refresh token
  Result: success
2026-03-06T03:58:10Z User signed in from 198.51.100.77 (unfamiliar)
2026-03-06T04:00:02Z Password changed by admin (ticket INC-4412)
logs.reading: A successful refresh-token sign-in from a new address minutes after an administrative password reset shows the token was never revoked. The reset did not evict the session. Revoke sessions and refresh tokens, then check what the token was used to access.

mcqs.question: A user's password was stolen through an adversary-in-the-middle phishing page that also captured the session cookie. What else is required beyond a password reset?
options: Nothing, a password reset ends the attacker's access
Revoke sessions and refresh tokens and review or reset registered MFA methods
Only enable sign-in risk alerts
Reimage the user's phone
mcqs.rationale: Cookie and token theft lets the attacker continue using an authenticated session after the password changes. Revoking sessions and tokens plus reviewing MFA registration removes the attacker's persistence; a password reset alone leaves it in place.

misconceptions.claim: A password reset closes a credential-theft incident.
misconceptions.correction: Refresh tokens, session cookies and Kerberos tickets can outlive a password change, and attacker-registered MFA methods can restore access. Eviction requires revoking sessions and tokens, reviewing authentication methods, rotating secrets and hunting for persistence.

facts.title: Insider threat: legal lead, security support, no tipping off
facts.fact: Insider cases split into negligent, compromised and malicious, and the response differs: a compromised employee is a victim who needs credential eviction, while a malicious insider is an HR and legal matter in which security provides evidence. HR and counsel normally lead, because employment law, works councils and privacy regulation constrain monitoring, searches and interviews, and because premature confrontation destroys evidence and can expose the organisation to claims. Security's job is to preserve lawfully collected evidence on company systems under existing policy, establish data movement through staging, removable media, printing and cloud sync, and keep the circle of knowledge small. Documentation must be strong enough for an employment tribunal, not only for a SOC ticket.
details: Behavioural precursors that are lawful to monitor include access outside role or hours, bulk downloads and resignation or disciplinary context.
Insider data often leaves through sanctioned channels such as personal cloud storage, email to self or printing rather than malware.
Chain of custody and reproducibility matter because the outcome may be reviewed by a tribunal rather than a security team.

mcqs.question: Security discovers an employee is staging large numbers of customer records in a personal cloud folder. Who should normally lead the response?
options: The SOC, because it detected the behaviour
HR and legal counsel, with security providing preserved evidence and technical context
The employee's line manager, who should confront them immediately
The communications team
mcqs.rationale: Insider cases are employment and legal matters constrained by privacy and labour law. HR and counsel direct the process and decide on interviews or disciplinary steps, while security preserves evidence and explains the technical findings. Immediate confrontation risks destroying evidence and creating legal exposure.

pitfalls: Confronting the employee before evidence is preserved and the legal strategy is agreed.
Using monitoring data collected outside the policy or without required consultation, which can make it unusable.

facts.title: Web compromise: webshells, skimmers and log-first triage
facts.fact: Web-server incidents usually present as defacement, a webshell, SEO spam, redirects or a payment-card skimmer injected into checkout pages. Triage starts with the access log: requests to unusual paths returning 200, POSTs of unusual size, odd user agents, and a small set of source addresses repeatedly hitting the same script. Preserve logs and a filesystem snapshot before the site is rebuilt or the WAF starts blocking, because blocking tells the actor they are observed and may prompt them to clean up their own tooling. Then scope persistence outside the web root - cron, systemd units, CMS plugins, database-stored templates, .htaccess and load-balancer configuration - and determine whether cardholder or personal data was exposed, which triggers PCI or privacy obligations.
details: Webshells are often small, lightly obfuscated and hidden among legitimate uploads; compare against a known-good file inventory.
A skimmer may live only in a database or template, so a filesystem diff alone can miss it.
Check for outbound connections from the web tier, which may indicate staging or a command channel.

logs.reading: A PHP file in an uploads directory receiving small POSTs that return large responses is a webshell pattern; a checkout fetch with a curl user agent from the same address suggests automated reconnaissance or skimmer verification. The response sizes indicate command output. Preserve the file and logs before removing it.

commands.purpose: Summarise successful PHP requests by source and path to surface unusual endpoints and heavy POST bodies.

mcqs.question: Why should web logs and a filesystem snapshot be captured before the WAF blocks the attacker's addresses?
options: Because logs are deleted automatically when a block rule is created
Because visible blocking can cause the actor to remove tooling and change infrastructure, destroying evidence value
Because WAF rules cannot be reversed
Because the snapshot is needed to restore service
mcqs.rationale: Blocking is a containment action that signals detection. Actors frequently delete webshells or move infrastructure once blocked, so evidence and scope should be captured first, then containment applied deliberately.

facts.title: Cloud incidents are identity-first and evidence is ephemeral
facts.fact: In cloud environments the control plane is the primary evidence and identity is the primary attack surface, so response starts by containing identities and access keys while preserving control-plane logs: AWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log with Entra sign-in and audit logs, and Google Cloud Audit Logs. Take disk and, where the provider supports it, memory snapshots before terminating an instance, because termination destroys local evidence and releasing an elastic address can break the association between an address and a host. Scope the blast radius through IAM: new users, access keys, role trust-policy changes, new service principals and resource policies that grant public access. Shared responsibility matters here: the provider secures the physical and hypervisor layers, while the customer owns identity configuration, data and workload logs.
details: CloudTrail's console event history covers 90 days of management events; longer retention requires a trail delivering to object storage.
Look for resource creation that indicates cryptomining or staging: many GPU instances, new VPCs, public buckets and shared snapshots.
Provider incident-response support routes and legal-process channels differ; know them before an incident.

configs.purpose: Illustrative CloudTrail management event showing the fields used to attribute an identity action.

mcqs.question: What is the most important first containment step for a suspected cloud account compromise?
options: Terminate every instance in the account
Contain the identity: disable or rotate credentials, revoke sessions and restrict permissions
Delete the account's VPCs to stop network access
Rotate all TLS certificates
mcqs.rationale: Cloud compromise is usually exercised through identities and APIs. Terminating instances destroys evidence, and network deletion is disruptive without stopping API access. Containing the identity and its keys, then scoping IAM changes, addresses the actual attack path.

pitfalls: Terminating the compromised instance before snapshotting it, losing the only local evidence.
Reviewing only the workload logs and missing the control-plane events that show how access was obtained and what was changed.

facts.title: Containment trade-offs: what each option costs you
facts.fact: Every containment action trades damage against visibility and evidence. Network isolation that keeps the EDR management channel alive preserves telemetry and remote triage; a full shutdown stops spread but destroys memory, may lose keys held only in RAM and, with some ransomware, can trigger additional damage on reboot. Disabling an account stops the actor but reveals the response, while disabling only the mailbox preserves the ability to watch. Perimeter blocking of command and control reduces harm but teaches the actor that the channel is burned, often causing a switch of infrastructure or acceleration of the objective. Monitoring-only containment is legitimate only with incident-commander and legal approval, a defined intelligence objective and an explicit exit condition.
details: Choose containment per actor objective: data theft calls for cutting exfiltration paths, while encryption calls for isolating file-sharing paths.
Record which trade-off was chosen and who approved it; post-incident review will ask.
Containment that cannot be sustained for the duration of the incident is not containment.

mcqs.question: Investigators want to observe an actor's command-and-control channel to identify additional victims. Which condition makes monitoring-only containment defensible?
options: The SOC analyst on shift thinks it is interesting
Incident commander and legal approval, a defined objective, and a clear exit condition with fallback containment
The channel uses HTTPS
The affected host is not business critical
mcqs.rationale: Deliberately leaving a channel open accepts ongoing risk. It requires accountable approval, a specific intelligence objective, monitoring that can detect escalation and a pre-agreed point at which containment is imposed.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

facts.title: Eradication is verification, not deletion
facts.fact: Eradication means removing the root cause and every access path the actor built, then proving it. Deleting the visible malware is the easy part; the work is enumerating persistence and access across identity, host, network and SaaS layers: local and domain accounts, scheduled tasks, services, WMI subscriptions, run keys, SSH authorized_keys, cron and systemd units, web shells, OAuth grants, API keys, VPN profiles and firewall rules. Rebuild rather than clean when compromise reached kernel level, when scope is not fully understood, or when the entry vector cannot be closed. Verification uses both indicator sweeps and behaviour-based hunting, because a competent actor will have changed indicators between visits.
details: Reset credentials from a clean host and in the right order, starting with identity infrastructure such as directory services and identity providers.
Patch or remove the entry vector before restoring access, or the actor returns through the same door.
Record negative findings with the query used, so verification is auditable rather than asserted.

commands.purpose: Enumerate non-Microsoft scheduled tasks as part of a persistence sweep.

mcqs.question: When is rebuilding a host preferable to cleaning it?
options: Whenever malware is detected, without exception
When compromise reached kernel level, scope is not fully understood, or the entry vector cannot be closed
Only when the host is a domain controller
When the user requests it
mcqs.rationale: Cleaning can be adequate when scope is understood and persistence is fully removed. Rebuilding is the safer choice when the compromise may be below the visibility line, when the extent is unknown, or when the original entry path remains open.

misconceptions.claim: Deleting the malware binary and running a full antivirus scan completes eradication.
misconceptions.correction: Eradication requires removing every access path the actor created, including accounts, tickets, scheduled tasks, services, WMI subscriptions, web shells, SSH keys, OAuth grants and cloud credentials. Scans only find known files; persistence and identity access usually survive them.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
ATT&CK: Scheduled Task/Job (T1053)

facts.title: Recovery validation and the heightened-monitoring window
facts.fact: Recovery is a controlled return rather than a switch-flip: restore in stages, verify the integrity of restored data and configuration, confirm the entry vector is closed, and only then reconnect to production networks. Run restored systems in an isolated environment long enough to observe whether they attempt to reach old infrastructure, and scan or rebuild backups rather than trusting them. Define a heightened-monitoring window with a named owner, specific detections to watch and a closing criterion, because 'we will keep an eye on it' decays within days. Business owners sign off on restoration of service; security signs off on the conditions attached to it.
details: Watch for re-entry attempts through the original vector, which is the best available test of eradication.
Validate that logging, EDR and backup agents are running on restored hosts before they carry traffic.
A shortened recovery that skips validation usually produces a second incident and a longer outage.

mcqs.question: Which element makes a heightened-monitoring period after recovery meaningful?
options: An open-ended commitment to watch alerts more closely
A named owner, specific detections, a defined duration and an explicit closing criterion
Disabling automated alerting to reduce noise
Returning all systems to service at once to restore productivity
mcqs.rationale: Open-ended monitoring erodes quickly and cannot be audited. A named owner, targeted detections, a fixed window and a closing criterion keep attention focused and make it possible to decide, with evidence, when the heightened period can end.

pitfalls: Restoring systems from backups that were never validated or scanned.
Reconnecting restored hosts before confirming that logging and endpoint agents are healthy.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
Federal Government Cybersecurity Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks

facts.title: Post-incident review: blameless, evidenced, tracked
facts.fact: A post-incident review held within about two weeks, while participants still remember decisions, produces a timeline, a list of what worked, what failed, and the detection and response gaps expressed as concrete changes. Keep it blameless about individuals while being precise about system failures, and tie findings to owners, dates and a tracking mechanism that someone actually reviews. Useful metrics include time from first evidence to detection, time to containment, dwell time and the proportion of the estate with usable telemetry, but any single metric can be gamed and mean time to recovery in particular can reward premature closure. Share a sanitised version so other teams learn without exposing victim details.
details: Map missed detections to ATT&CK techniques to expose coverage patterns rather than one-off gaps.
Distinguish 'the control failed' from 'the control was never deployed', because the fixes differ.
Verify that closed action items are effective, not merely marked done in the tracker.

mcqs.question: Why can mean time to recovery (MTTR) be a misleading incident metric on its own?
options: It is impossible to measure
It can reward premature closure and ignores whether the root cause was removed or the actor evicted
It only applies to cloud incidents
It is always higher than dwell time
mcqs.rationale: A team can shorten MTTR by restoring service before eradication is verified, leaving the organisation exposed to reinfection. MTTR needs to be read alongside detection time, eradication evidence and recurrence rates.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management

facts.title: Tabletop exercises must test decisions, not trivia
facts.fact: A tabletop exercise walks a realistic scenario through the people who would actually make decisions, using timed injects that force choices under incomplete information: who declares, who calls legal, whether to isolate a revenue system, what is said to customers. The point is to surface friction in authority, contact data, tooling access and communication, so the exercise must include executives, communications, legal and business owners, not only the SOC. Discussion-only exercises are cheap and repeatable; functional and red-team exercises validate that tools and procedures work when executed. Record gaps as findings with owners, and re-test the same scenario later to confirm improvement.
details: Injects should escalate: a second host, a journalist call, a regulator deadline and a backup that will not restore.
No-fault ground rules increase candour; blaming participants produces a rehearsed performance instead of a test.
Measure decision latency and information flow, not how many facts participants can recall.

configs.purpose: Illustrative exercise plan with timed injects and explicit objectives to test decisions rather than knowledge.

mcqs.question: Which outcome indicates a tabletop exercise was well designed?
options: Participants answered all technical questions correctly
The exercise revealed unclear decision rights or contact failures before a real incident
The scenario was resolved within the scheduled hour
No disagreements occurred between teams
mcqs.rationale: Exercises exist to find friction in authority, contact data, tooling and communication. Friction discovered in a tabletop is a success, because it can be fixed cheaply; a smooth run with no findings often means the scenario was not demanding enough.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61r3: Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
Federal Government Cybersecurity Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks

facts.title: Contemporaneous documentation is evidence and memory
facts.fact: A single incident log, with UTC timestamps, the person acting, the action taken, the evidence reference and the reason, is the backbone of both coordination and legal defensibility. Contemporaneous notes carry far more weight than reconstructions written afterwards, so record decisions and negative findings as they happen, including 'checked source, found nothing, query attached'. Keep chat exports, ticket links, hashes and screenshots tied to the log, avoid editorialising or speculation, and distinguish observed fact from inference. During handover the log is what keeps the next shift from repeating work or destroying evidence.
details: Use one authoritative timeline and link sub-timelines to it rather than maintaining several competing ones.
Record who authorised destructive or disruptive actions, and when.
Note tool versions and query text so results can be reproduced by another analyst.

mcqs.question: Which entry is most useful in an incident log?
options: 'Isolated host, seemed bad'
'10:42Z j.okoro isolated host-fs02 from the server VLAN per IC approval (INC-4412), memory image captured first, hash recorded'
'Attacker was probably an insider'
'Waiting on vendor'
mcqs.rationale: A defensible entry records time in UTC, actor, action, authorisation, evidence handling and case reference. Vague impressions ('seemed bad', 'probably') are not reproducible and may prejudice later analysis or legal review.

misconceptions.claim: The team will remember what happened, so a detailed log can be written at the end.
misconceptions.correction: Memory degrades within hours and is reconstructed to fit the outcome. Contemporaneous notes capture sequence, authorisation and negative findings, and they are the records that survive scrutiny in reviews, tribunals and regulatory enquiries.

references.title: NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
RFC 3227: Guidelines for Evidence Collection and Archiving

facts.title: Order of volatility drives collection sequence
facts.fact: RFC 3227 recommends collecting evidence from most to least volatile: CPU registers and cache, memory, network state and traffic, running processes, then disk, then remote logs and monitoring data, then archival media and paperwork. The rationale is simple: a process table or ARP cache may be gone in seconds, while a powered-off disk keeps its contents for years. Collection should be planned so that acquiring one item does not destroy another, since memory capture writes to disk and packet capture competes for bandwidth, so sequence and tooling are chosen together. Business continuity and physical safety override strict volatility order, and the report should say when that happened.
details: Container and cloud workloads add ephemeral layers: a container filesystem may vanish with the pod while the node disk persists.
Record the system clock, time zone and uptime before collection, then convert to UTC for the timeline.
If a host must stay running for business reasons, state the constraint and what evidence was therefore lost or degraded.

commands.purpose: Capture clock, uptime, network state and process list before any disruptive action on a live host.

mcqs.question: According to RFC 3227's order of volatility, which should generally be collected first?
options: The hard disk image
CPU registers, cache and memory
Archival backups
Printed documentation
mcqs.rationale: RFC 3227 orders collection from most to least volatile, starting with registers and cache, then memory, network state, running processes and only later disk and archival media, because volatile state disappears fastest.

misconceptions.claim: The safest first action on a suspected compromised host is to pull the power.
misconceptions.correction: Powering off destroys memory-resident evidence such as running processes, network state, injected code and keys, and can trigger destructive behaviour on next boot. Capture volatile data first and isolate at the network layer; power removal is a last resort that should be documented as such.

references.title: RFC 3227: Guidelines for Evidence Collection and Archiving

facts.title: Disk imaging: write blocking, hashing and verification
facts.fact: A forensic image is a sector-level copy of the source, taken through a write blocker so the original is never modified, with a hash of the source computed and matched against the image. Raw images in the dd style are simple and universally readable; the EnCase Evidence File (E01) format adds compression, case metadata and per-block checksums; AFF4 provides an open specification with similar integrity features. Document the tool and version, source device identifiers, hash algorithm, bad sectors or read errors, and destination media, because an image with unexplained gaps is a weak exhibit. Work from the verified copy and keep the original sealed.
details: For large or failing media, use a tool that logs read errors instead of silently substituting zeros.
Verify the image hash after transfer to analysis storage, not only at acquisition.
For live systems, targeted or logical collection may be more appropriate than a full image, but state which was done and why.

commands.purpose: Acquire a raw image with a logged SHA-256 and an error log for later review.

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of a write blocker during disk acquisition?
options: To speed up the imaging process
To prevent any write operation from modifying the source evidence
To encrypt the resulting image
To compress the image to save space
mcqs.rationale: A write blocker permits reads while blocking writes, so the source device is not altered during acquisition. Speed, compression and encryption are separate properties of imaging tools and formats.

references.title: NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
The Sleuth Kit

facts.title: Memory evidence: what it holds and how it is acquired
facts.fact: Memory holds process lists, command lines, network connections, injected code, encryption keys, clipboard and chat fragments, and unpacked malware that never touches disk. Acquisition uses a kernel driver such as WinPmem on Windows or LiME on Linux, a hardware device, or a hypervisor snapshot, and each method perturbs the system to some degree. Hibernation files and pagefile or swap contents provide partial, time-shifted memory images. Analysis with Volatility 3 needs the symbol table matching the exact kernel build, which is why capturing build information alongside the image matters; a mismatched profile produces plausible but wrong results.
details: Record the acquisition tool and version, hash, uptime and clock offset with the image.
Encrypted volumes yield keys from memory only while mounted, so capture before locking or shutting down.
Memory analysis can recover malware configuration without executing the sample.

commands.purpose: List processes from a Windows memory image with Volatility 3.
List network endpoints and owning processes from a memory image.

mcqs.question: Why must the kernel build be known when analysing a Windows memory image with Volatility 3?
options: Because the image is encrypted with a build-specific key
Because symbol tables are version-specific, and a mismatch yields plausible but incorrect results
Because Volatility can only read images smaller than 4 GB
Because the tool requires a licence per build
mcqs.rationale: Volatility resolves kernel structures through symbol tables tied to a specific build. Using the wrong profile produces output that looks valid but misinterprets structure offsets, which can silently corrupt findings.

references.title: Volatility 3 documentation
NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

facts.title: Network evidence: packets, flows and the limits of each
facts.fact: Full packet capture provides content and protocol detail but is expensive to store and often retained for days, while flow records such as NetFlow, IPFIX and cloud VPC flow logs provide metadata for weeks or months with no payload. Zeek turns a packet feed into connection, DNS, HTTP and TLS logs, which is often the most analysis-friendly form for incident work. Correlation requires handling NAT and load balancers, because one internal address may map to many external sessions, and it requires a trustworthy time source across capture points. TLS 1.3 traffic is opaque without session keys, so metadata and endpoint telemetry carry the investigation.
details: Check capture-point placement: a span port that misses inter-VLAN traffic creates blind spots that look like absence of activity.
DNS logs often reconstruct command-and-control and tunnelling better than proxy logs alone.
Preserve captures with hashes and record the capture filter, interface and drop counters.

commands.code: tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'dns' -T fields -e frame.time_utc -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name | head -50
commands.purpose: List DNS queries with UTC timestamps from a capture for beaconing and tunnelling review.

logs.reading: Near-identical request size, response size and roughly five-minute spacing to a single rare destination is a beacon pattern. The small variance is jitter. Pivot to the process on 10.20.30.41 making these connections, then check other hosts for the same domain or TLS fingerprint.

mcqs.question: Which source is most likely to preserve evidence of internal lateral movement that full packet capture missed due to a span-port gap?
options: Flow records from routers and switches
The host's prefetch files
Printed network diagrams
The domain controller's SYSVOL share
mcqs.rationale: Flow metadata from network devices records connections even when payload capture was incomplete, and it is often retained longer. Prefetch shows local execution but not the network path, and the other options carry no connection history.

references.title: NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
tshark manual page

facts.title: Timelines: normalise, then interpret
facts.fact: A timeline is a derived artifact: each source has its own clock, precision and semantics, so normalising everything to UTC and recording source and precision per event prevents false conclusions. NTFS timestamps have 100-nanosecond resolution but update with documented and undocumented rules, FAT has two-second granularity, and application logs may record local time without an offset. Plaso (log2timeline) builds super-timelines across dozens of artifact types, and psort filters and orders them; mactime from The Sleuth Kit handles filesystem MACB times. The analyst's job is to explain gaps and contradictions, not to smooth them away.
details: MACB means modified, accessed, changed (MFT entry change) and born (creation), each with different update behaviour.
Clock skew and time-zone misconfiguration are common on virtual machines and appliances; compare against an external reference.
A single-source timeline is a story; a multi-source timeline is evidence.

commands.purpose: Build a Plaso storage file from a disk image for super-timeline analysis.
Export a filtered CSV timeline beginning at a chosen UTC date.

mcqs.question: Why should each timeline event record its source and precision?
options: To satisfy chain-of-custody requirements only
Because different sources have different clock accuracy, granularity and update semantics, which affects interpretation
Because tools refuse to merge events without it
To make the output smaller
mcqs.rationale: An event accurate to two seconds and an event accurate to 100 nanoseconds cannot be ordered with equal confidence, and application clocks may be skewed. Recording source and precision lets the analyst weigh contradictions instead of over-reading the sequence.

references.title: Plaso documentation
NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

facts.title: MFT timestamps: $STANDARD_INFORMATION versus $FILE_NAME
facts.fact: Every NTFS file has a record in $MFT with two attribute sets carrying four timestamps each: $STANDARD_INFORMATION (0x10), which normal file APIs update, and $FILE_NAME (0x30), which is updated on rename and on parent-directory changes. Timestomping tools typically rewrite $STANDARD_INFORMATION and leave $FILE_NAME inconsistent, so a creation time later than the $FILE_NAME creation time, or sub-second values of exactly zero, is a strong indicator of manipulation. Conversely $FILE_NAME times can legitimately lag, so a mismatch is a lead to corroborate with $LOGFILE, $UsnJrnl and event logs rather than proof on its own.
details: Resident files store content inside the MFT record; large files use $DATA runs pointing to clusters.
Alternate data streams appear as additional $DATA attributes and can survive simple copy operations in some tools.
$MFT records can also be carved from unallocated space, sometimes recovering deleted file metadata.

commands.purpose: Extract the $MFT record stream from an image with a 2048-sector offset.
Parse the extracted MFT into CSV for timestamp comparison.

mcqs.question: An executable's $STANDARD_INFORMATION creation time is 2026-03-04, but its $FILE_NAME creation time is 2024-11-12. What is the best interpretation?
options: The file was definitely created twice
A mismatch consistent with timestomping, to be corroborated with other artifacts before concluding
The disk has hardware failure
NTFS stores random values in $FILE_NAME
mcqs.rationale: Tools that alter timestamps commonly change $STANDARD_INFORMATION only, leaving $FILE_NAME behind. The mismatch is a strong lead, but $FILE_NAME can also lag for legitimate reasons, so it must be corroborated with $UsnJrnl, $LogFile or event logs.

references.title: NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
Eric Zimmerman's forensic tools documentation (MFTECmd)

facts.title: USN journal: change history that timestomping does not erase
facts.fact: The NTFS USN change journal ($Extend\$UsnJrnl:$J) records file system changes with a monotonically increasing update sequence number, the file reference, reason flags such as FILE_CREATE, DATA_EXTEND, RENAME_OLD_NAME, RENAME_NEW_NAME and 0x80000000 for FILE_DELETE, and usually a timestamp. It is a rolling log bounded by maximum size, so older records are overwritten, and an administrator can delete it with fsutil, which is itself a notable anti-forensics action. Because some records carry unreliable timestamps, analysts map USN ranges to time using $MFT, $LogFile or event logs. Its main value is ordering: it shows what changed around an event even when MFT timestamps were altered.
details: $UsnJrnl has two streams: $J holds the change records and $Max holds journal metadata such as maximum size and allocation delta.
Reason flags accumulate, so one record may list several changes for the same operation.
Journal deletion is inferred from the absence of expected records plus any command telemetry or event logs covering the deletion.

commands.purpose: Read the USN journal on a live Windows host without modifying it.

mcqs.question: Why is the USN journal useful when an attacker has timestomped files?
options: It stores a copy of every file's content
It records an ordered sequence of file system changes with reason flags, independent of the timestamps an attacker edited
It encrypts file names so they cannot be changed
It replaces the need for a disk image
mcqs.rationale: The journal records ordered change events with reasons and file references. Even where per-record timestamps are missing or unreliable, that ordering can be anchored to other artifacts and contradicts a fabricated file timeline.

references.title: fsutil usn
NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

facts.title: Prefetch: execution evidence with clear limits
facts.fact: Windows Prefetch files (.pf) in C:\Windows\Prefetch record an executable's name, run count, up to eight recent run times, referenced files and volumes, and are written by the Prefetch/SysMain component shortly after a program starts. They are valuable for showing that a binary ran, where it ran from and what it loaded, but absence proves little: execution can finish before the trace is written, the service may be disabled, cleanup tools delete the files, and Windows Server disables prefetch by default. Windows 10 and 11 retain up to about 1024 entries, so older entries are evicted on busy systems.
details: Prefetch files on Windows 8 and later can be parsed with tools such as PECmd, which handle the compressed format.
A prefetch entry for a binary in a temp path with a run count of one and a volume serial matching a USB device is a strong lead.
Prefetch does not record command-line arguments; pair it with process creation events for those.

commands.code: Get-ChildItem C:\Windows\Prefetch\*.pf | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 20 Name,LastWriteTime
commands.purpose: List the most recently written prefetch files on a live host.

mcqs.question: A host has no prefetch entry for a binary that event logs show was executed. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The event log entry must be forged
Prefetch absence is inconclusive: the service may be disabled, the entry evicted, or the write not completed
The binary never executed
The binary was deleted before execution
mcqs.rationale: Prefetch is best-effort telemetry with a bounded store, and it is disabled by default on Windows Server. Absence cannot refute execution evidence from other sources; it only means this artifact does not record it.

references.title: Eric Zimmerman's forensic tools documentation (PECmd)
NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

facts.title: Amcache and ShimCache answer different questions
facts.fact: Amcache.hve in C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve is a registry hive recording application inventory: paths, first-seen and link timestamps, publisher and version from version resources, and for many executables a SHA-1 file identifier, with entries persisting after the file is deleted. ShimCache, the AppCompatCache value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager, records compatibility-shim observations and is best treated as evidence of presence, not execution; some Windows 10 builds add a last-modified time that can support an execution argument, but semantics vary by build. Neither is a reliable last-executed record, and neither replaces prefetch or event logs, but together they survive file deletion and are strong leads about what existed on a host.
details: Amcache's FileId is a SHA-1 of file content for many entries, allowing hash-based pivoting without the file itself.
Parsing Amcache requires the hive plus knowledge of the Windows build, because value names and structure changed across versions.
ShimCache entries are not stored in chronological order and should not be used to rank execution.

commands.purpose: Export the SYSTEM hive, which contains ShimCache, for offline analysis.

mcqs.question: Which statement about ShimCache is most accurate?
options: It records an ordered list of every program executed with timestamps
It primarily evidences that a file existed or was examined, and its execution semantics vary by Windows build
It stores copies of executable content for later analysis
It is deleted whenever a file is deleted
mcqs.rationale: ShimCache is a compatibility-shim artifact. It evidences presence or examination of a binary, and only some builds include a last-modified time that can support an execution inference. It is unordered, holds no content copy, and does not guarantee execution.

references.title: NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
Eric Zimmerman's forensic tools documentation (AppCompatCacheParser, AmcacheParser)

facts.title: SRUM records per-application network and resource usage
facts.fact: The System Resource Usage Monitor stores data in C:\Windows\System32\sru\SRUDB.dat, an Extensible Storage Engine database, with hourly records per application: bytes sent and received, interface, user SID, and CPU or energy counters depending on version. For exfiltration questions it can show which process moved volume and under which account, even after the process has exited, and it can corroborate a cloud-sync or backup tool as the data path. Records are pruned on a rolling basis, roughly 30 to 60 days on Windows 10 and 11 depending on activity, so it complements rather than replaces proxy and firewall logs. Parsing requires the ESE database plus the SOFTWARE hive to resolve SIDs and application names.
details: Volume alone is not exfiltration: backups, updates and video calls move large amounts of data legitimately.
Correlate SRUM bytes with destination logs to establish where the data went, not just how much.
The database is locked on a running system; collect it with the hives and a volume image, or from an image.

mcqs.question: What question is SRUM best suited to answer?
options: Which user typed a specific command
Which application sent or received a given volume of network data in a time window and under which account
What the contents of a deleted file were
Which TLS cipher suite was negotiated
mcqs.rationale: SRUM aggregates per-application resource and network usage per hour, attributed to a user SID. It shows volume and application, not command lines, file contents or cipher details, so it is used to corroborate exfiltration volume and timing.

references.title: srum-dump
NIST SP 800-86: Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response

facts.title: Linux: journald, auditd and login records
facts.fact: systemd-journald writes structured binary journals; with Storage=auto and a /var/log/journal directory present it persists them, otherwise logs live in /run/log/journal and vanish on reboot, so a host without persistent storage loses its own history. journalctl filters by unit, boot, priority and time, and the journal typically includes the process, PID, unit and a monotonic timestamp useful for ordering. auditd records syscall and policy events to /var/log/audit/audit.log under rules in /etc/audit/rules.d, which makes it the better source for file access, privilege changes and execve arguments when the rules cover them; ausearch and aureport query it. Login history lives in wtmp, btmp and lastlog, which are binary and rotated.
details: auditd captures execve arguments only if the rule includes them, and default rule sets vary by distribution.
journald can forward to a remote collector, which preserves events if the host is wiped.
A stopped auditd service or a permissive journald configuration is itself an indicator worth investigating.

commands.purpose: Query persistent journal entries for a unit within a precise UTC window.

mcqs.question: A Linux host's journal contains only entries since its last boot. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The journal was encrypted
Journal storage is volatile because /var/log/journal does not exist, so records live under /run and are lost on reboot
auditd was disabled
The kernel does not support logging
mcqs.rationale: With Storage=auto, journald persists only when the persistent journal directory exists; otherwise it writes to the volatile runtime path and the history disappears at reboot. That is a configuration gap, not encryption or a kernel limitation.

references.title: systemd-journald.service manual
auditd(8) manual page

facts.title: Bash history: useful, incomplete and easy to lose
facts.fact: Shell history is a convenience log, not an audit trail: it is written when the shell exits, so a killed session may leave nothing, and HISTFILE can be unset, redirected to /dev/null or pointed elsewhere. HISTCONTROL=ignorespace drops commands prefixed with a space and ignoredups collapses repeats; HISTIGNORE filters patterns; HISTSIZE caps the in-memory list; and timestamps appear only if HISTTIMEFORMAT was set when the commands were entered. Running history -c clears the in-memory list and, depending on histappend, may or may not truncate the file on exit, so the file itself must be checked. Other shells behave differently, since zsh's extended history stores timestamps and durations, and non-interactive execution records nothing at all, which is why process accounting and auditd matter.
details: Commands run by scripts, cron jobs and service managers generally never reach bash history.
Check per-user files, root's file, and any HISTFILE override in shell profiles.
Deleted history can sometimes be recovered from disk slack or backups, but not reliably.

commands.purpose: Display the most recent commands with timestamps where the shell recorded them.
Count stored history entries in a user's history file.

mcqs.question: Which command is least likely to appear in bash history?
options: An interactive command typed at a prompt
A command run by a cron job's non-interactive shell
A command preceded by a space with HISTCONTROL=ignorespace
A command entered before the shell exits normally
mcqs.rationale: Non-interactive shells generally do not write history at all, so scripted and scheduled execution leaves no history record. Space-prefixed commands are also dropped when ignoredups or ignorespace is set, and normal interactive commands are recorded at exit.

misconceptions.claim: If a command is not in .bash_history, it was never run.
misconceptions.correction: History is written at shell exit, can be disabled or redirected, drops space-prefixed and duplicate commands depending on configuration, is truncated by HISTSIZE, and never captures non-interactive execution. Absence is not evidence of non-execution; auditd, process accounting and application logs cover those gaps.

facts.title: Anti-forensics indicators worth hunting
facts.fact: Anti-forensic activity is often easier to detect than the activity it hides, because the cleanup is itself logged somewhere. High-value indicators include Security event 1102 (audit log cleared) and System event 104, a USN journal deleted or disabled, the event log service stopped or its size reduced, auditd stopped or its rules flushed, prefetch and Amcache entries missing for binaries that clearly ran, timestamps inconsistent between $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME, secure-deletion or free-space wiping tools, shell history replaced by a symlink to /dev/null, and Sysmon or EDR agents uninstalled or silenced. Absence of evidence must be corroborated: a log gap can equally come from a retention policy, a full disk or a failed agent.
details: Centralised logging is the main defence, because an attacker must then tamper in two places.
Tamper protection and signed agent configurations raise the cost of disabling telemetry.
Correlate with authentication events, since cleanup usually requires privileged access.

logs.context: Windows Security and System logs after suspected cleanup
logs.text:

The audit log was cleared

facts.title: Forensic soundness is a method claim, not a feeling
facts.fact: Forensic soundness means the process is documented, repeatable and minimally invasive, with validated tools and preserved originals, so an independent examiner could reproduce the findings. ISO/IEC 27037 describes identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of digital evidence; the NIST Computer Forensics Tool Testing programme publishes test reports and methodologies for imaging tools and write blockers; peer review and recorded tool versions close the loop. Soundness is not the same as admissibility: admissibility is decided by a court under its own rules, such as the Daubert factors in US federal courts, and a technically sound examination can still be excluded for procedural reasons such as an unrecorded break in custody.
details: Keep contemporaneous notes with enough detail for someone else to repeat each step.
Record known limitations, failed reads and tool errors rather than presenting a clean narrative.
Validate that a write blocker actually blocks writes in the configuration used, not merely that one was purchased.

mcqs.question: Which pair of concepts is correctly distinguished?
options: Soundness and admissibility are the same thing
Soundness concerns documented, repeatable and minimally invasive method; admissibility is a legal determination by a court
Admissibility is decided by the forensic tool vendor
Soundness only applies to criminal cases
mcqs.rationale: Soundness is a methodological property that supports reliability, while admissibility depends on legal rules and the judge's assessment. A sound examination can be excluded on procedural grounds, and an unsound one is vulnerable to challenge even in a civil or internal process.

misconceptions.claim: A matching hash proves the evidence is authentic and the findings are correct.
misconceptions.correction: A hash proves integrity from the point of hashing. Authenticity also depends on lawful and documented collection, and the correctness of findings depends on validated tools, sound interpretation and review. Integrity is necessary but not sufficient.

facts.title: Browser and SaaS logs: short retention, high value
facts.fact: Browser forensics reads SQLite databases such as Chrome and Edge History, Downloads, Cookies and Login Data, and Firefox places.sqlite and cookies.sqlite, plus cache and session files, which can show what a user visited, downloaded or uploaded and when, subject to sync and private-browsing gaps. Cloud and SaaS sources are equally important and expire quickly: Entra ID sign-in logs are typically retained for about 30 days, AWS CloudTrail's console event history covers 90 days of management events, and Microsoft 365 unified audit log retention is measured in months and varies by licence. Export to a SIEM or case store early, because once the retention window closes the evidence is gone regardless of any legal hold.
details: Browser timestamps are often microseconds since 1601 (WebKit) or Unix epoch; convert carefully and confirm against a known event.
Chrome's History database is locked while the browser runs, so copy it before opening.
Cloud audit logs record the API caller identity, source address and user agent, which often distinguishes console use from automated access.

commands.purpose: List recent Chrome or Edge history entries with converted timestamps from a copied profile database.

mcqs.question: Why must cloud audit logs be exported rather than relied on in place?
options: They are encrypted and cannot be read by customers
Provider retention windows are short and expire independently of any legal hold you issue
They only record failed requests
They are deleted whenever a user changes their password
mcqs.rationale: Retention is set by the provider and licence, typically 30 days for Entra sign-in logs and about 90 days for CloudTrail console history. A legal hold on your side cannot extend the provider's window, so forward the logs to storage you control.

facts.title: Static and dynamic analysis answer different questions
facts.fact: Static analysis examines a sample without running it: hashes, file type, strings, PE or ELF headers, imports, resources, signatures and YARA matches. It is safe, fast and repeatable, but packing, encryption and obfuscation defeat it. Dynamic analysis runs the sample in an instrumented, isolated environment and observes process, file, registry, network and memory behaviour, revealing intent that static inspection cannot, at the cost of time and of the sample detecting the environment. Practitioners loop between the two: static findings suggest what to watch for dynamically, and dynamic findings tell the analyst where to look in the code. Triage always starts with hashing and reputation lookup so known-good or already-characterised files are not re-analysed.
details: Record the SHA-256, file size, type and first-seen time before any other action.
YARA rules match structural and string patterns and are useful for family classification and hunting across stores.
Never open a sample on a production workstation, and treat documents with macros or exploits as live until proven otherwise.

commands.code: sha256sum sample.bin; file sample.bin; strings -n 8 sample.bin | head -40
commands.purpose: Fingerprint a sample and extract readable strings for a first-pass assessment.
Match a sample against a directory of local YARA rules.

mcqs.question: What is the main limitation of static analysis alone?
options: It is slower than running the sample
It requires internet access for every sample
Packing, encryption and obfuscation can hide imports, strings and behaviour from inspection
It can only be performed on Linux
mcqs.rationale: Static inspection reads what is present in the file. Packers and crypters compress or encrypt the real code and rebuild imports at runtime, so the meaningful content may not exist in a readable form until execution.

facts.title: Reading a PE file's structure for triage
facts.fact: A Windows PE file starts with the MZ DOS header, whose e_lfanew field points to the PE signature, followed by the COFF file header (machine, section count, timestamp, characteristics) and the optional header (entry point, image base, subsystem, DLL characteristics such as ASLR, DEP and CFG, and data directories for imports, exports, resources and the certificate table). Section headers map names such as .text, .rdata, .data and .rsrc to virtual addresses, raw offsets and permissions; a section that is both writable and executable, or whose raw size is far smaller than its virtual size, suggests self-modifying or unpacking code. Imports reveal capability such as crypto, networking and process-injection APIs, exports reveal DLL purpose, TLS callbacks execute before the entry point, and an absent or invalid Authenticode signature is a lead rather than proof of malice.
details: The compile timestamp in the COFF header is trivially forged and should be treated as a hint only.
Check the resource directory for embedded executables and the overlay for appended data.
Rich header and PDB path strings sometimes leak build tooling and development paths.

commands.code: python3 -c "import pefile,sys; pe=pefile.PE(sys.argv[1]); print(hex(pe.OPTIONAL_HEADER.AddressOfEntryPoint)); [print(s.Name, hex(s.Characteristics)) for s in pe.sections]" sample.exe
commands.purpose: Print the entry point and section characteristics of a PE file with pefile.

mcqs.question: A PE section has raw size 512 bytes but virtual size 96 KB, and its characteristics mark it writable and executable. What does this most suggest?
options: The file is definitely benign because it is small
A likely unpacking stub that expands code into memory at runtime
The file is a text document with an unusual extension
The signature is valid
mcqs.rationale: A large virtual-to-raw size ratio plus write-and-execute permissions is a classic packer pattern: the stub is tiny on disk and allocates a much larger executable region at runtime. It is a lead requiring behavioural confirmation, not proof of malice.

facts.title: Reading an ELF binary's structure for triage
facts.fact: An ELF file begins with 0x7f 'E' 'L' 'F', a class byte (32 or 64 bit), an endianness byte and a type: ET_EXEC for a fixed-address executable, ET_DYN for a position-independent executable or shared object, and ET_REL for a relocatable object. Program headers describe loadable segments (PT_LOAD), the interpreter (PT_INTERP) and dynamic linking (PT_DYNAMIC); section headers name .text, .data, .rodata, .init_array and .fini_array, where init-array functions run before main. Imports appear as undefined dynamic symbols and in the PLT and GOT, a stripped binary keeps dynamic symbols but loses local names, and static linking hides library dependencies entirely. Linux malware frequently ships as a stripped ET_DYN with an unusual interpreter path or as a script wrapper that drops and runs a payload.
details: Use objdump -p to list needed libraries rather than ldd on an untrusted binary, because some loader implementations can execute code when resolving dependencies.
Check for an unusual PT_INTERP path, which can indicate a custom loader.
High-entropy sections and a very small set of imports are packer indicators on ELF as on PE.

commands.purpose: Inspect ELF header, program headers and section headers of a sample.
List shared-library dependencies without invoking the dynamic loader.

mcqs.question: What does an ELF e_type of ET_DYN indicate?
options: A relocatable object file that cannot be executed
A position-independent executable or shared object
A core dump
A 32-bit binary
mcqs.rationale: ET_DYN means the object is position independent and can be loaded at a chosen base address, which covers shared libraries and PIE executables. Relocatable objects are ET_REL, core dumps are ET_CORE, and bit width is recorded separately in the class byte.

facts.title: Packer and obfuscation indicators
facts.fact: Packing compresses or encrypts the original code and prepends a stub that unpacks it at runtime, so static strings and imports shrink to almost nothing while entropy rises. Reliable indicators include section entropy above roughly 7.0 bits per byte, very few imports (often only LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress), writable-and-executable sections, unusual or duplicated section names, a large gap between raw and virtual sizes, an entry point outside the first section, and a data overlay. UPX is identifiable by its UPX0 and UPX1 section names and can often be unpacked with upx -d if unmodified, but custom packers and crypters require behavioural analysis instead. Detection should not depend on unpacking, because file, registry and network behaviour survives packing.
details: Compute entropy per section rather than per file, so a packed section is not diluted by resources.
Memory analysis after execution often recovers the unpacked image and configuration.
Legitimate installers and software protectors also pack code, so entropy alone is not malicious.

commands.code: python3 -c "import collections,math,sys;d=open(sys.argv[1],'rb').read();c=collections.Counter(d);print(-sum(v/len(d)*math.log2(v/len(d)) for v in c.values()))" sample.bin
commands.purpose: Compute the Shannon entropy of a file to support a packing assessment.
List UPX compression metadata if the file is a standard UPX-packed binary.

mcqs.question: Which combination is most consistent with a packed executable?
options: High section entropy, very few imports, and a writable-executable section
Low entropy and a large, diverse import table
A valid Authenticode signature and a version resource
Many readable strings referencing documentation URLs
mcqs.rationale: Packing hides strings and imports and expands code at runtime, producing high entropy, a minimal import table and often an executable writable region. A rich import table and readable strings suggest unpacked code; a signature and version resource indicate nothing about packing.

misconceptions.claim: If a sample will not unpack, it cannot be analysed or detected.
misconceptions.correction: Unpacking is an analysis convenience, not a detection requirement. Behaviour such as persistence, injection, file encryption and network check-in is observable without the original code, and memory capture often recovers the unpacked image and configuration.
