facts.title: Command and control patterns: beaconing, jitter and covert channels
facts.fact: Implant check-in behaviour is one of the most durable detection surfaces because it is hard to change without losing resilience. Typical patterns are periodic connections with jitter (for example a nominal 60-second interval randomised by about 20 percent), long-lived TLS sessions to rare destinations, uniform request sizes, a consistent user agent, and fallback to a second channel when the first fails. Abuse of DNS through TXT or NULL queries and high-volume subdomains, HTTPS to newly registered or unpopular domains, domain fronting and DNS over HTTPS are all common, and the last two hide the true destination from network inspection. Detection combines statistical periodicity, destination rarity and reputation, JA3, JA3S and JARM fingerprints, and endpoint evidence of the process making the connections.
details: Jitter defeats naive fixed-interval detections, so use variance-tolerant scoring over long windows.
A proxy log showing identical bytes out and in at regular intervals is a classic beacon signature.
Blocking one channel often triggers the fallback, which is itself a detection opportunity.

logs.context: Zeek conn.log excerpt for a suspected implant
logs.reading: Identical payload sizes (412 out, 318 in), short sessions and approximately five-minute spacing with small variance to one external address indicate scripted check-in. Because the payload is uniform, this is likely a fixed-format heartbeat rather than interactive traffic. Pivot on the JA3 fingerprint and the local process.

mcqs.question: Why does beacon jitter make fixed-interval detection less effective?
options: It encrypts the traffic so intervals cannot be measured
It randomises the timing around a base interval, so exact-period matching misses the connections
It changes the destination address on every connection
It uses UDP so no connection records exist
mcqs.rationale: Jitter spreads check-in times around a mean, breaking rules that look for exact periodicity. Detection still works using statistical measures of regularity over longer windows, combined with rarity and fingerprinting.

facts.title: Living-off-the-land binaries: signed tools, hostile intent
facts.fact: Living-off-the-land techniques use binaries already present and often signed by the operating system, such as certutil, bitsadmin, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32, wmic, msbuild, installutil and PowerShell on Windows, and curl, wget, bash, python, tar and systemctl on Linux, so allow-listing by file reputation fails. The signal is context: a signed binary fetching a remote payload, spawning an unexpected child, writing to a temp directory, or making its first-ever outbound connection. Detection therefore needs command-line visibility, parent-child baselines and egress monitoring for processes that should not have network access, which is why process creation auditing and Sysmon event 1 are foundational controls. Removing interpreters and proxy-execution binaries that the business does not need reduces the surface substantially.
details: Microsoft's system binary proxy execution techniques (T1218) are the canonical Windows examples.
On Linux, memfd-based execution and interpreter one-liners achieve similar deniability.
Baseline which signed utilities are normal in your estate; 'never seen in this parent' is more useful than a global blocklist.

The parent being cmd.exe from an interactive user session suggests scripted activity. Check what ran next, whether the file executed, and whether the same host contacted the address again.

mcqs.question: Why is file-signature allow-listing insufficient against living-off-the-land techniques?
options: Signed binaries cannot be executed by non-administrators
The binaries are legitimate and signed, so only behaviour and context distinguish malicious use
Signatures are always invalid on Windows
The technique requires kernel drivers
mcqs.rationale: LOTL abuses binaries that are already trusted and present, so reputation checks pass. Detection must rely on command-line content, parent-child relationships, unexpected network egress and file writes for a tool that normally does none of those things.

facts.title: Ransomware encryption behaviour and where to detect it
facts.fact: Ransomware typically generates a per-file symmetric key using AES or ChaCha20, wraps it with an asymmetric public key embedded in the binary, encrypts file content and often renames files with a family extension while dropping a ransom note in each directory. To increase speed, several families observed in 2022 and 2023 encrypt only part of each file, which lowers CPU cost and changes the write pattern analysts expect. Precursor behaviour is more detectable than encryption itself: shadow-copy deletion, backup service tampering, disabling recovery, mass renames by an unusual process and a sharp rise in write volume. Defensive controls that change outcomes are canary files, write-rate alerting on file servers, immutable backups and tested restore.
details: Partial encryption often preserves file headers, so magic-byte checks may still succeed on damaged files.
Deleted shadow copies remove local recovery but not offsite or immutable copies; verify both.
A ransom note is useful evidence but is not required for detection.

logs.context: Windows file server, object access auditing and EDR

  Object: D:\shares\finance\Q1.xlsx  Access: WriteData (or AddFile)  Process: encryptor.tmp.exe
  Subject: EXAMPLE\svc-backup
4663 events in 60s: 1874

logs.reading: A single non-standard process writing to many finance documents at high rate, under a service account, with high-entropy output is encryption in progress. Isolate the server's network path, preserve memory, and check whether the same account or binary touched other shares.

mcqs.question: Which precursor is most useful for detecting ransomware before encryption begins?
options: The presence of a ransom note
Deletion of volume shadow copies and tampering with backup or recovery services
The file extension of encrypted files
High CPU use on a workstation
mcqs.rationale: Shadow-copy deletion and backup tampering typically precede encryption and are strong, specific signals. Ransom notes and renamed extensions appear only after encryption, and CPU use is too generic to be reliable.

misconceptions.claim: Backups on a domain-joined backup server are sufficient protection against ransomware.
misconceptions.correction: Ransomware operators routinely target backup infrastructure with the same stolen domain credentials. Protection requires immutable or offline copies, separate credentials and management planes, and verified restore tests, not merely a second server in the same domain.

facts.title: Fileless techniques and the telemetry that catches them
facts.fact: Fileless execution keeps payloads out of ordinary files: PowerShell download cradles and encoded commands, WMI event subscriptions for persistence, payloads stored in the registry, reflective DLL or .NET assembly loading, process injection through remote threads, APC queues or process hollowing and, on Linux, memfd_create followed by execution from /proc/self/fd or a binary in /dev/shm. Because nothing malicious is written to disk, detection shifts to script block logging in PowerShell event 4104, module and image loads, process access events, network connections from interpreters and memory scanning. Command-line and parent-process telemetry remain the highest-yield sources, and application control plus constrained language mode raises the cost of the technique.
details: Sysmon events 7 (image loaded), 8 (CreateRemoteThread), 10 (process access) and 25 (process tampering) target injection behaviour.
Base64 in a command line is not proof of malice, but it is a strong reason to decode and review.
Memory-resident payloads may be recoverable from a crash dump or a full memory image.

commands.purpose: Review recent PowerShell script block logging events for suspicious script content.

mcqs.question: Which event source most directly exposes a PowerShell script that was decoded and executed only in memory?
options: Security event 4624
PowerShell script block logging, event 4104
System event 7045
Windows Update log
mcqs.rationale: Script block logging records the script text as it is compiled, including deobfuscated content in many cases, which is exactly what disk-based file scanning misses. 4624 is a logon, 7045 a service install, and the update log is unrelated.

facts.title: Sandbox results are a signal, not a verdict
facts.fact: Sandboxes are easy to evade: samples sleep past the analysis window, check for virtual-machine artifacts, low CPU counts, small disks, analysis tooling or a non-domain-joined host, wait for user interaction, require a specific geolocation, or fetch a second stage only from a live command-and-control server the sandbox cannot reach. A clean report therefore means no observed behaviour in that environment, not benign. Compensating practices include bare-metal or customised analysis hosts, longer runtimes, simulated internet services that answer DNS and HTTP, multiple sandboxes from different vendors, and memory and network capture during execution. The most useful output is often the configuration or infrastructure revealed during execution, which feeds detection even when the verdict is wrong.
details: Record the sandbox vendor and version, runtime and network simulation profile with the result.
Compare behaviour across at least two engines before trusting a benign verdict.
Samples that detect analysis often reveal the detection technique itself, which is useful intelligence.

mcqs.question: A file returns a clean report from one sandbox. What is the sound conclusion?
options: The file is benign
No malicious behaviour was observed in that environment, which is not proof of benignity
The file is definitely packed
The sandbox licence has expired
mcqs.rationale: Evasion through sleeping, environment checks or staged delivery means a clean report is only an absence of observed behaviour. Corroborate with other engines, longer runs, simulated services and static or memory analysis before concluding.

misconceptions.claim: A clean sandbox verdict clears the file, so it can be released to users.
misconceptions.correction: Sandbox evasion is routine and a clean run only describes that environment and time window. Release decisions should weigh provenance, static findings, other engines and user context, and a single clean report is not a clearance.

facts.title: The intelligence cycle and the actions it must support
facts.fact: Threat intelligence is produced through a cycle: direction and planning, which establishes what decision the product must inform; collection; processing and normalisation; analysis; dissemination in a form the consumer can act on; and feedback that redirects the next cycle. In practice the cycle is iterative, with analysis constantly sending new requirements back to collection. A product without a stated consumer and decision is research rather than intelligence, and a product whose format does not match the consumer's workflow will be ignored. Good intelligence states what is known, how it is known, how confident the judgement is and what decision it supports.
details: Direction should name the decision, the deadline and the classification level of the product.
Dissemination format follows the consumer: detection content for a SOC, exposure assessment for a CISO, risk narrative for a board.
Feedback is a requirement, not a courtesy; it is how collection priorities change.

mcqs.question: Which element turns a research report into threat intelligence?
options: It contains at least one IP address
It is produced for a specific consumer and decision, with sourcing and confidence stated
It is longer than ten pages
It is classified
mcqs.rationale: Intelligence is defined by its use in a decision. Naming the consumer and decision, stating provenance and confidence, and formatting for the workflow are what make a product actionable rather than interesting background reading.

facts.title: The pyramid of pain: why TTPs outlast indicators
facts.fact: David Bianco's pyramid of pain ranks indicator types by the difficulty they cause an adversary when defenders detect and block them: file hashes are trivial to change, IP addresses easy, domain names harder, network and host artifacts cost more, tools cost more still, and tactics, techniques and procedures are the most painful because changing them changes how the actor operates. The practical implication is that detection engineering should climb the pyramid: a hash block catches one sample, while behaviour detection for credential dumping catches the technique across families. The pyramid is a prioritisation heuristic, not a measurement, and low-level indicators remain valuable for retro-hunting and for scoping an incident already in progress.
details: Hashes are still essential for confirming a known sample and finding copies across the estate.
Indicator durability generally rises with abstraction, but so does false-positive risk.
Track which pyramid level each detection rule depends on to see how brittle coverage is.

mcqs.question: Why are TTP-based detections considered more durable than hash-based detections?
options: TTPs are easier to write as signatures
Changing a technique is costly for an adversary, whereas a hash changes with any trivial modification to the sample
Hashes cannot be computed on modern systems
TTPs never produce false positives
mcqs.rationale: A single byte change alters a hash, so hash blocking is defeated by repacking. A technique such as credential dumping requires the actor to change methodology, tooling and often infrastructure, which is far more disruptive and therefore more durable to detect.

misconceptions.claim: Because TTPs are at the top of the pyramid, indicators are worthless and should not be collected.
misconceptions.correction: The pyramid ranks the adversary's cost to change, not the defender's value per case. Indicators are the fastest way to confirm a known sample, sweep an estate and scope an incident, and they feed the behavioural analytics that sit higher up.

facts.title: Using ATT&CK without technique bingo
facts.fact: MITRE ATT&CK describes adversary behaviour as tactics, meaning the adversary's goal, with 14 tactics in the Enterprise matrix; techniques and sub-techniques identified as T#### and T####.###; and procedures, the specific implementations observed. It also lists mitigations as M#### and, in recent versions, detection guidance. Mapping supports coverage analysis, detection engineering, threat-informed defence and communication, but it is easy to abuse: one action can serve several tactics, telemetry often supports only part of a technique, and mapping from memory produces drift. Record the ATT&CK version used, the evidence behind each mapping and the sub-technique where it matters, and keep mappings in a versioned Navigator layer so coverage can be compared over time.
details: Pre-compromise, host and post-compromise tactics are separate; coverage of one says nothing about another.
Group and software pages give real procedures that make abstract techniques concrete.
Express defensive coverage as 'we can detect this sub-technique with this data source at this confidence'.

mcqs.question: Why should an ATT&CK mapping record the ATT&CK version used?
options: Because techniques are added, split and renamed across versions, so coverage comparisons are misleading without it
Because MITRE requires a licence per version
Because Navigator cannot open layers without a version
Because older versions are illegal to use
mcqs.rationale: ATT&CK evolves: sub-techniques are added, names change and content is revised. A coverage score from one version cannot be compared meaningfully with another unless both are recorded, which is why layers carry a version and a date.

facts.title: STIX 2.1 and TAXII 2.1: the plumbing of sharing
facts.fact: STIX 2.1 is an OASIS standard JSON model for cyber threat information: STIX Domain Objects such as indicator, malware, campaign, intrusion set, threat actor, report and observed data; STIX Relationship Objects such as relationship and sighting; and STIX Cyber-observable Objects such as IPv4 address, domain name, file with hashes, process and network traffic. Indicators carry a pattern in the STIX patterning language and a validity window, and objects carry created and modified times plus UUID identifiers. TAXII 2.1 is the transport: HTTPS APIs organised into API roots and collections that consumers poll or subscribe to. Much operational sharing still uses CSV or proprietary feeds, so normalisation into STIX loses fidelity unless it is done deliberately.
details: STIX IDs are UUIDs; deterministic UUIDv5 generation keeps stable identifiers across versions of the same object.
Indicator valid_from and valid_until express expiry, which many consumers ignore when importing.
A STIX bundle is only a container and has no transport semantics of its own.

configs.purpose: Illustrative STIX 2.1 bundle with an indicator pattern and an explicit validity window.

mcqs.question: What is the relationship between STIX and TAXII?
options: STIX is the transport protocol and TAXII is the data model
STIX defines the data model for threat information, while TAXII defines a transport API for exchanging it
They are competing data models for the same purpose
Both are proprietary formats owned by MITRE
mcqs.rationale: STIX describes what is shared: objects, relationships and observable patterns. TAXII describes how it is shared over HTTPS, through API roots and collections. Both are OASIS standards, and neither is a MITRE product.

facts.title: Confidence, provenance and handling markings
facts.fact: Intelligence judgements need three things that are often conflated: source reliability, information credibility and analytic confidence. The Admiralty system rates sources A (completely reliable) to F (cannot be judged) and information 1 (confirmed by other sources) to 6 (cannot be judged); analytic confidence, commonly low, moderate or high, describes how strongly the evidence supports the judgement, and none of these is a probability. Provenance records where each fact came from, when it was collected, by what method and what corroborates it, so a consumer can re-evaluate it. Handling markings are separate again: TLP 2.0 defines CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER+STRICT and RED, and governs sharing rather than classification or legal sensitivity, so a TLP marking never substitutes for a privacy or data-handling assessment.
details: 'High confidence' without stated evidence cannot be falsified and should be rejected in review.
Record first-seen and last-seen for infrastructure, because an IP address changes owners and meaning over time.
Commercial feeds rarely expose their sourcing; treat unprovenanced indicators as leads, not facts.

mcqs.question: An indicator is marked TLP:AMBER. What does that tell you?
options: It is classified at the same level as national-security information
It may be shared within the recipient's organisation on a need-to-know basis, but not publicly or with outside organisations without the source's permission
It may be posted to any public blocklist
It has been confirmed by three independent sources
mcqs.rationale: TLP is a sharing convention. AMBER limits distribution to members of the recipient's organisation who need it, and TLP 2.0's AMBER+STRICT narrows this further to the organisation only. Neither marking says anything about classification level or evidentiary confidence.

facts.title: Feed quality, indicator expiry and the cost of auto-blocking
facts.fact: A threat-intelligence feed is only as good as its precision for your environment: a list of IP addresses that includes CDN ranges, NAT egress points, public resolvers or shared hosting will cause outages if auto-blocked, and a hash list that includes benign installers will cause false positives. Evaluate feeds on provenance, freshness, coverage, deduplication, false-positive history and whether indicators carry context such as role, first-seen date and associated campaign. Indicators decay at different rates: an IP may be reassigned in days, a domain may persist for months, a hash lasts until the sample is repacked, and a TTP may stay relevant for years, so every indicator needs an expiry or review date. Mature programmes stage new indicators in alert-only mode, measure precision, then promote to blocking.
details: Store indicators with a confidence score, a source, a TTL and an owner, and query by expiry before blocking.
Prefer domain and TLS fingerprint blocking over IP blocking where shared infrastructure is common.
Track the operational cost of blocks, since helpdesk tickets are a concrete precision signal.

commands.code: SELECT indicator, type, source, confidence, expires_at FROM intel_indicators WHERE expires_at < now() ORDER BY expires_at;

mcqs.question: Why is auto-blocking IP addresses from a commercial feed risky?
options: IP addresses cannot be blocked at firewalls
Shared infrastructure such as CDNs, resolvers and NAT gateways means a blocklist entry can affect legitimate services and many users
IP addresses never appear in threat feeds
Firewalls cannot store more than 100 rules
mcqs.rationale: An IP address is not a stable identity. Shared hosting, CDNs and carrier NAT mean one address serves many benign parties, so blocking it can cause outages. Alert-only staging and context review reduce this risk.

facts.title: Attribution: evidence, aliases and false flags
facts.fact: Attribution is an analytic judgement, not a property of an indicator: shared tooling, leaked builders, common infrastructure providers and copied tradecraft mean technical overlap supports association, not identity. Actors deliberately plant false flags, operate through criminal proxies or share infrastructure with other groups, and vendor naming multiplies aliases for the same cluster, so one intrusion set may carry a country-designation name, a vendor animal name and a private tracker's number. ATT&CK separates intrusion sets, which are observed activity clusters, from threat actors, the underlying organisations, precisely because the link between them is inferential. Public attribution carries legal, diplomatic and safety consequences and should follow organisational policy rather than an analyst's blog post.
details: State the confidence and the alternative hypotheses, including 'a different actor using the same tool'.
Infrastructure overlap is weakest when the infrastructure is commodity or cloud-hosted.
Keep a cross-reference table of aliases and the sources that assert each mapping.

mcqs.question: Two campaigns use the same custom backdoor. What is the strongest defensible conclusion?
options: The same individual conducted both campaigns
The campaigns are associated through shared tooling, which is one input to attribution but not proof of a common operator
Both campaigns were conducted by the same nation state
The backdoor was bought from the same vendor, proving a single buyer
mcqs.rationale: Tool sharing is evidence of association, not identity. Builders leak, tools are sold and shared, and actors plant or inherit artifacts. Attribution needs corroboration across infrastructure, tradecraft, targeting and timing, with an explicit confidence level.

pitfalls: Publishing an actor name before legal and policy review, creating commitments the organisation cannot support.
Treating an infrastructure overlap with a commodity cloud provider as a strong link.

misconceptions.claim: A TLP:RED marking means the information is classified secret.
misconceptions.correction: TLP is a sharing convention, not a classification scheme. RED means the information is limited to the named recipients and must not be redistributed; classification level and legal handling obligations are separate determinations made by the source organisation.

facts.title: Sanitising intelligence before you share it
facts.fact: Sharing incident intelligence safely means removing what identifies the victim or exposes them to further harm: customer and employee names, internal hostnames and addresses, usernames, file paths that reveal business structure, and contract or project names, while preserving the technical facts that make the intelligence useful. Replace identifiers with consistent synthetic values so relationships remain readable, keep malware hashes and structural detection logic intact, and check metadata that travels invisibly, such as document properties, EXIF data, packet-capture payloads and screenshots. Apply the correct TLP marking, obtain legal or privacy review where personal data or contractual obligations are involved, and share through a trusted channel such as a sector ISAC or an access-controlled MISP instance.
details: Hashes of malware are not personal data and usually remain shareable; internal addresses and hostnames are the common leak.
Packet captures can contain credentials, session cookies and personal content even when the attack traffic looks clean.
Sanitisation must not change meaning: a rewritten indicator that no longer matches is worse than none.

mcqs.question: Which item most needs removal before sharing an incident report outside the organisation?
options: The SHA-256 of the malware sample
A spreadsheet of internal hostnames, usernames and customer identifiers
The ATT&CK technique identifiers
The detection rule logic
mcqs.rationale: Victim-identifying data such as internal names, usernames and customer identifiers can cause harm and may breach privacy obligations. Hashes, technique IDs and generic detection logic are the technical value of the report and normally stay.

misconceptions.claim: Changing every indicator to a synthetic value is always the safest way to sanitise a report.
misconceptions.correction: Over-sanitisation destroys the utility that justified sharing. Hashes, malware family names and generic logic should be preserved; only victim-identifying and sensitive context needs replacement, and replacements must keep relationships consistent.

facts.title: Initial access: the techniques and the controls that matter
facts.fact: ATT&CK groups initial access into phishing (T1566, with attachment, link and service-based sub-techniques), exploitation of public-facing applications (T1190), external remote services such as VPN and RDP (T1133), valid accounts (T1078), removable media (T1091), supply-chain compromise (T1195) and drive-by compromise (T1189). Controls that change outcomes are phishing-resistant MFA for remote access and email, prompt patching of internet-facing systems with priority for the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, restricting exposed management interfaces, and mail filtering with attachment detonation. Detection leans on mail-gateway and authentication logs: a first-ever successful VPN login from a new country, or a logon through a residential proxy for an account that normally works from one city, is often the earliest signal.
details: Phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2 or passkeys defeats real-time adversary-in-the-middle phishing in a way that one-time codes do not.
Exploitation often leaves no malware, so web access logs and server-side process creation are the evidence.
Valid-account access produces no exploit signature, which is why identity baselines carry the detection.

2026-03-01T08:02:11Z vpn01 user=a.nguyen src=10.20.30.55 result=success method=saml mfa=push geo=GB
2026-03-03T02:47:39Z vpn01 user=a.nguyen src=198.51.100.19 result=success method=saml mfa=push geo=NL device=unknown
2026-03-03T02:49:10Z vpn01 user=a.nguyen src=198.51.100.19 bytes_out=1843200 dst=10.20.40.12:445
logs.reading: The same account authenticates from a new country, on an unknown device, at an unusual hour, then immediately makes an SMB connection to an internal file server. That sequence suggests credential use rather than the legitimate user, and the SMB destination makes it a lateral-movement lead as well. Check MFA method changes and mailbox rules for the account.

mcqs.question: Which control most directly mitigates real-time adversary-in-the-middle phishing that relays a session?
options: Longer passwords
Phishing-resistant MFA bound to the origin, such as FIDO2 security keys or passkeys
Disabling email entirely
Increasing password rotation frequency
mcqs.rationale: Relay phishing defeats OTP and push-based MFA because the attacker proxies the real session. Origin-bound cryptographic authenticators will not authenticate to the attacker's proxy domain, so the credential material cannot be relayed.

facts.title: Execution: interpreters, user action and what to log
facts.fact: Execution techniques cover command and scripting interpreters (T1059: PowerShell, Windows Command Shell, bash, VBScript, Python and JavaScript), user execution of malicious files or links (T1204), Windows Management Instrumentation (T1047), scheduled tasks and cron (T1053) and exploitation for client execution (T1203). The detection foundation is process creation with command lines: Security event 4688 with command-line auditing enabled, or Sysmon event 1, gives parent, child, user, path and arguments. Script-level visibility comes from PowerShell script block logging, event 4104, and AMSI, which expose obfuscated or in-memory scripts that never appear as a file. Mitigations that raise cost are application control through WDAC or AppLocker, constrained language mode, macro blocking and removing interpreters the business does not need.
details: 4688 command-line capture is off by default and must be enabled by policy; without it most of this telemetry is missing.
Look for interpreter processes whose parent is an Office application, a web server or a database service.
Script block logging often records the deobfuscated script, which is why it is high value.

commands.purpose: Inspect recent process-creation events when command-line auditing is enabled.

mcqs.question: Why is Security event 4688 often incomplete for execution analysis?
options: It only records failed logons
Command-line inclusion is disabled by default, so the event may show the process name but not its arguments
It is only generated on domain controllers
It stores only the parent process
mcqs.rationale: 4688 is generated when process creation auditing is enabled, but command-line content requires a separate policy setting. Without it the event still proves a process started, but not what it was told to do.

misconceptions.claim: Enabling PowerShell logging is enough to catch script-based execution.
misconceptions.correction: Module, script block and transcription logging each capture different things, and none of them sees commands run through other interpreters such as cmd, mshta, wmic or python. Execution coverage needs process creation with command lines, application control and network egress monitoring together.

facts.title: Persistence: enumerating every place an actor can return from
facts.fact: Persistence is broad by design: registry Run keys and startup folders (T1547.001), Windows services (T1543.003), scheduled tasks (T1053.005), WMI event subscriptions (T1546.003), local and domain account creation (T1136), account manipulation including SSH authorized_keys (T1098.004), web shells (T1505.003), systemd services and timers (T1543.002), cron (T1053.003) and shell profile modification (T1546.004). A credible sweep covers all of these plus cloud identity persistence such as new app registrations, OAuth grants, access keys and federation changes. Mitigations include restricting service and task creation to administrators, application control, monitoring autoruns, and maintaining an expected baseline so new entries stand out. Detection based only on file names fails against renamed or signed binaries.
details: Compare installed services and tasks against a golden baseline rather than reviewing thousands of entries by hand.
Scheduled tasks can be triggered by logon, idle, boot or a WMI event, so the trigger is as interesting as the action.
Cloud persistence often survives endpoint reimaging entirely.

commands.purpose: List services whose binaries live outside the Windows directory.

mcqs.question: Which persistence mechanism is most likely to survive a full endpoint reimage?
options: A registry Run key
A malicious service binary in Program Files
A newly registered OAuth application in the cloud identity provider
A scheduled task stored locally
mcqs.rationale: Identity-provider objects such as OAuth grants, app registrations and federation settings live outside the endpoint, so reimaging the laptop does not remove them. The other options are all on-host and are destroyed by reimaging.

facts.title: Privilege escalation and credential access: the escalation chain
facts.fact: Privilege escalation and credential access usually run together: exploitation for privilege escalation (T1068), abuse of elevation control such as UAC bypass or sudo misconfiguration (T1548), access token manipulation (T1134), hijacking of execution flow through DLL search order or unquoted service paths (T1574) and then credential dumping from LSASS, SAM or NTDS.dit (T1003), password stores (T1555), unsecured files (T1552) or Kerberos abuse such as Kerberoasting and AS-REP roasting (T1558). Defences are architectural: LSA protection through RunAsPPL, Credential Guard, a tiered administrative model, just-in-time administration, disabling NTLM where feasible, managed service accounts and removing standing local administrator rights. Detection relies on process access to LSASS, service and task creation, unusual ticket requests and the first appearance of administrative tooling on a workstation.
details: Logon type 9 (NewCredentials) and event 4648 indicate explicit credential use and are worth baselining.
Kerberoasting appears as service ticket requests using weak encryption types for accounts that should never be requested.
Credential Guard moves secrets out of LSASS but does not fix misconfigured privileges or over-broad group membership.

configs.purpose: Registry setting that enables LSA protection so LSASS runs as a protected process (requires reboot and compatible drivers).

mcqs.question: Which control most directly limits the value of a successful LSASS memory dump?
options: Increasing the minimum password length
Credential Guard, which isolates derived credential material from LSASS
Disabling USB ports
Enabling Windows Firewall
mcqs.rationale: Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to keep derived secrets out of LSASS, so a dump yields far less usable material. Password length helps against guessing but not against memory theft, and the other options do not address credential storage.

misconceptions.claim: Kerberoasting requires domain administrator rights to perform.
misconceptions.correction: Kerberoasting can be performed by any authenticated domain user: it requests service tickets for accounts with service principal names and attacks the ticket offline. That is why service accounts need long, randomly generated passwords or group managed service accounts, and why ticket requests for unused SPNs are worth alerting on.

facts.title: Lateral movement, C2 and exfiltration: the network story
facts.fact: After a foothold, actors move with remote services (T1021: RDP, SMB and admin shares, SSH, WinRM and VNC), transfer tooling (T1570), then communicate and exfiltrate over application-layer protocols (T1071: web, DNS, mail), encrypted channels (T1573), ingress tool transfer (T1105), exfiltration over alternative protocols (T1048), over web services (T1567) and over the command-and-control channel (T1041). Detection depends on knowing normal internal and egress flows: SMB or WinRM from workstation to workstation, administrative-share access by a non-admin account, first-seen internal host pairs, service creation on a remote host (event 7045), and outbound sessions with large sustained uploads. Mitigations are segmentation, host firewalls, LAPS to make local admin passwords unique, restricted admin shares, egress allowlists and, where lawful, TLS inspection or metadata analysis.
details: Logon type 3 (network) and type 10 (RemoteInteractive) with a source workstation name are the classic 4624 lateral-movement records.
Beaconing and exfiltration can share a channel; volume and timing distinguish them.
Cloud storage uploads may bypass proxy inspection entirely, so CASB or SaaS audit logs are needed.

logs.context: Windows Security event 4624, network logon with workstation attribution
logs.text:
2026-03-03T02:51:04Z host-fs01 Security 4624
  LogonType: 3  TargetUser: EXAMPLE\svc-backup
  WorkstationName: WS-0442  IpAddress: 10.20.30.88
  AuthenticationPackage: NTLM  ImpersonationLevel: Impersonation
  2026-03-03T02:51:05Z host-fs01 Security 5140 share=\\*\ADMIN$ accessed by EXAMPLE\svc-backup from 10.20.30.88
logs.reading: A backup service account authenticating from a workstation, over NTLM, to the ADMIN$ share is not normal backup behaviour. Workstations should not drive backup service authentications. Pivot to 10.20.30.88, check what process initiated the connection, and look for service creation on host-fs01 around the same time.

mcqs.question: Which pattern is the strongest lateral-movement signal on a Windows estate?
options: A user logging on interactively at their own desk
A workstation authenticating over SMB to another workstation's administrative share
A server contacting a patch repository
A laptop connecting to the corporate VPN
mcqs.rationale: Workstation-to-workstation administrative share access inverts normal tiers and is a common propagation path. Interactive logon at one's own desk and patch or VPN traffic are expected behaviours.

facts.title: Defence evasion and impact: what the endgame looks like
facts.fact: Before impact, actors impair defences (T1562: disabling antivirus, tampering with logging, uninstalling agents) and remove indicators (T1070: clearing Windows event logs, deleting files, modifying timestamps), often by modifying the registry (T1112) or abusing signed system binaries (T1218). Impact techniques include inhibiting system recovery (T1490, deleting shadow copies or disabling recovery), data encrypted for impact (T1486), service stop (T1489), data destruction and manipulation (T1485, T1565) and denial of service (T1498). The defensive counterweight is tamper-resistant telemetry: protected EDR configuration, near-real-time log forwarding off the host, and immutable or offline backups. A cleared Security log (event 1102) is both an attack indicator and a gap in your evidence, which is why centralised collection is a control rather than a convenience.
details: Tamper protection in Microsoft Defender and equivalent EDR features should be enabled, and its state monitored centrally.
Shadow-copy deletion is a pre-impact signal that often precedes encryption by minutes to hours.
Test that log forwarding survives the loss of a domain controller or the compromise of the SIEM's credentials.

logs.context: Mixed host telemetry during defence evasion
logs.text:
2026-03-04T03:10:02Z host-dc01 System 7036 The Windows Event Log service entered the stopped state.
2026-03-04T03:11:20Z host-dc01 Security 1102 The audit log was cleared.
2026-03-04T03:12:02Z host-dc01 System 7045 Service installed: WinDefendHelper
2026-03-04T03:14:33Z host-dc01 Defender: real-time protection disabled by policy (unexpected)
logs.reading: Stopping the log service, clearing the audit log, installing a masquerading service and disabling real-time protection within four minutes is a coordinated defence-evasion sequence, not administrative maintenance. Check whether the actions came from a legitimate change ticket, and rely on forwarded copies of the logs for the preceding events.

mcqs.question: Which control best preserves evidence when an actor clears the local Security log?
options: Larger local log files
Near-real-time forwarding of events to a separate collector
Encrypting the local disk
Daily full backups of the host
mcqs.rationale: Clearing affects the local log, but events already forwarded to a remote collector survive. Larger files only delay the clear and backups may capture an already-cleared log, so forwarding is the control that defeats this technique.
